extracted.intended_audience: Citizens and policymakers debating ratification and design of a federal Constitution (explicitly addressed to the People of New York)
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidance and evaluative criteria for structuring a national (federal) government capable of preserving the Union, maintaining defense and public peace, regulating commerce, and administering justice. The text argues which powers, institutional arrangements, and procedural safeguards are necessary and why.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judiciary: one supreme tribunal
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws are a dead letter without courts to expound and define their true meaning and operation. To produce uniformity in these determinations, they ought to be submitted, in the last resort, to one SUPREME TRIBUNAL.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treaties and other laws must be ascertained by judicial determinations; if each State has a court of final jurisdiction there may be as many different final determinations as courts. A single paramount court is necessary to avoid contradictory decisions, local bias, and to establish a uniform rule of civil justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treaties as part of national law
rubrics_metrics.description: The treaties of the United States, to have any force at all, must be considered as part of the law of the land.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The true import of treaties, as far as they affect individuals, must be ascertained by judicial determinations and therefore fall under the jurisdiction of the supreme tribunal; treaties should be instituted under the same authority which forms them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Energetic federal government necessary to preserve the Union
rubrics_metrics.description: The necessity of a Constitution, at least equally energetic with the one proposed, to the preservation of the Union is asserted as a central point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inquiry divides into (1) objects to be provided for by the federal government, (2) quantity of power necessary, and (3) the persons upon whom power should operate. Once the need for a federal government is accepted, it must be vested with all powers requisite to the complete execution of its trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects for federal government
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal purposes to be answered by union are: the common defense of the members; the preservation of the public peace as well against internal convulsions as external attacks; the regulation of commerce with other nations and between the States; the superintendence of our intercourse, political and commercial, with foreign countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These objects define the domains in which the national government must be empowered, and the scope of authority should match these substantive responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Powers essential to the common defense
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorities essential to the common defense are: to raise armies; to build and equip fleets; to prescribe rules for the government of both; to direct their operations; to provide for their support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These powers ought to exist without limitation because it is impossible to foresee or define the extent and variety of national exigencies; the means must be coextensive with possible combinations of circumstances affecting national safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means proportioned to ends
rubrics_metrics.description: The MEANS ought to be proportioned to the END; the persons, from whose agency the attainment of any END is expected, ought to possess the MEANS by which it is to be attained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A government entrusted with particular objects must be given coincident powers sufficient to achieve those objects; failing to confer adequate means violates prudence and imperils national interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal laws must operate directly on individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: We must extend the laws of the federal government to the individual citizens of America; we must discard the fallacious scheme of quotas and requisitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislating through State quotas and requisitions is impracticable and unjust; direct federal authority over individuals ensures effective execution of national laws and avoids reliance on potentially unwilling or biased state legislatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal authority to levy troops and raise revenues
rubrics_metrics.description: The Union ought to be invested with full power to levy troops; to build and equip fleets; and to raise the revenues which will be required for the formation and support of an army and navy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such powers should be exercisable in the customary and ordinary modes practiced in other governments; the federal government must be able to raise resources and forces without depending on state compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper organization of Congress for federal powers
rubrics_metrics.description: A single assembly may be a proper receptacle of those slender, or rather fettered, authorities which have been heretofore delegated to the federal head; but it would be inconsistent with all the principles of good government to intrust it with those additional powers which ought to reside in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess institutional structure by whether it is fit to be trusted with the powers needed; if a proposed plan's internal structure renders it unworthy of public confidence it should be rejected. Avoid concentrating all important prerogatives of sovereignty in an improperly designed single body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundation: consent of the people
rubrics_metrics.description: The fabric of American empire ought to rest on the solid basis of THE CONSENT OF THE PEOPLE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ratification resting solely on state legislatures exposes the national system to questions about validity and even the doctrine of legislative repeal; direct consent of the people provides deeper legitimacy and stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rigid constitutional restraints on military discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: Restraints upon the discretion of the legislature in respect to military establishments in time of peace would be improper to be imposed, and if imposed, from the necessities of society, would be unlikely to be observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A constitutional prohibition on standing armies or on raising armies in peacetime would incapacitate the nation from preparing for defense and create ambiguities about what constitutes 'keeping up' troops; allowing legislative discretion is pragmatically necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-year appropriation limit as a safeguard
rubrics_metrics.description: That clause which forbids the appropriation of money for the support of an army for any longer period than two years is a precaution which... will appear to be a great and real security against the keeping up of troops without evident necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A periodic appropriation requirement provides a practical guard against permanent armies while preserving the legislature's ability to respond to changing threats.

rubrics_metrics.name: National control of military to prevent state rivalries
rubrics_metrics.description: If objects of defense were left to State governments, some States (e.g., New York) would bear disproportionate burdens and others would be tempted to provide counterbalancing forces; separate possession of military forces by the States would foster rivalries and threaten the Union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Centralized national possession and management of military forces promotes equity, avoids mutual jealousy that would enlarge and misuse forces, and prevents States from becoming engines for abridging or demolishing national authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional standing forces preferable to militia for effective defense
rubrics_metrics.description: The militia would not long submit to be dragged from their occupations... The steady operations of war against a regular and disciplined army can only be successfully conducted by a force of the same kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reliance solely on militia is impractical and dangerous; permanent (though possibly small) professional corps and garrisons are often necessary for frontier defense, protection of dockyards and arsenals, and effective response to regular armies.
